title: Cell-Based Architecture and Limiting Blast Radius
lesson:
A cell-based architecture partitions a service into many independent, identical copies called cells, each with its own compute, data store, and queues, and serving only a fixed subset of customers. A thin routing layer maps each customer (or tenant) to exactly one cell. The goal is to limit blast radius: if a bad deploy, poisoned request, or capacity problem takes down one cell, only the customers assigned to it are affected, instead of the entire fleet.

This differs from ordinary horizontal scaling, where all instances share the same database and dependencies, so one failure can cascade everywhere. In a cell design nothing is shared across cells on the request path, and cells are sized to a known maximum so they are well tested at that scale. Capacity grows by adding more cells, not by making a cell larger, which also makes performance predictable.

The router is the part that must stay shared, so it has to be extremely simple, highly available, and ideally stateless, using a small mapping such as a hash or lookup table from customer ID to cell. Deployments pair naturally with cells: roll a change to one cell first, watch its health, and only then continue, which turns every release into a small canary. A noisy or suspicious customer can also be moved into its own cell.

The tradeoffs are real: more operational units to manage, lower resource utilization because each cell needs headroom, and difficulty with operations that cross customers, such as global reporting or customers who need to interact. Cells fit best when failures are expensive and tenancy partitions cleanly.

questions.prompt: What is the primary benefit of a cell-based architecture?
options: Limiting the number of customers affected by a failure
Eliminating the need for a routing layer
Sharing one database to simplify operations
questions.explanation: Independent cells confine failures to a fraction of customers, shrinking the blast radius.

questions.prompt: In a cell-based design, all cells should share one central database so data stays consistent.
questions.explanation: Sharing a datastore reintroduces a common dependency, so one failure can still affect every cell.

questions.prompt: The shared component that maps each customer to its cell is called the ____ layer.
questions.explanation: A thin router is the only shared piece, which is why it must be kept simple and highly available.

questions.prompt: How does a cell architecture usually add capacity?
options: Add more cells of a fixed, well-tested size
questions.explanation: Cells are kept at a known size so scaling means adding cells, keeping behavior predictable.

questions.prompt: Order a cell-aware rollout, earliest first.
items: Roll back if the cell degrades or proceed otherwise
questions.explanation: A release hits one cell, is observed, gets a go or no-go decision, and only then spreads.
